title: Istanbul 2005
standfirst: Follow Liverpool and AC Milan from kick-off through the half-time change, the comeback and the final’s resolution. Pause to examine the teams, roles and evidence at each moment.

blocks.text: Liverpool and AC Milan meet at the Atatürk Olympic Stadium in Istanbul on 25 May 2005, with the European Cup to be decided in one final. Rafael Benítez names Jerzy Dudek in goal and Milan Baroš in attack; Carlo Ancelotti's side includes Paolo Maldini, Andrea Pirlo, Kaká, Andriy Shevchenko and Hernán Crespo. Harry Kewell starts for Liverpool, with Dietmar Hamann among the seven named substitutes. These are the players available at the beginning, before injuries and replacements alter the choices.

Liverpool's route has run through qualifying, a group and three knockout rounds. They have overcome Grazer AK, finished second in their group and eliminated Bayer Leverkusen, Juventus and Chelsea. Fourteen European matches, including qualifying, have brought them here. The road below keeps those stages together: the final is a new match at 0–0, but the route explains why Olympiacos, Juventus and Chelsea already carry such significance in this campaign.

Begin with the two teams, or follow the match forward. At the interval, pause to compare the personnel Benítez still has with the side that restarts. The question is how Liverpool can find a way back while containing a Milan attack that will demand attention throughout the evening. The formations shown here are explanations of roles, with their sources and limits attached. The named teams and the changes to them come from the match record.

Milan lead in the first minute. Pirlo delivers a free-kick and Maldini meets it to beat Dudek. The score is already Liverpool 0–1 Milan: Liverpool must now find a goal while facing the threat of conceding again. The official event record gives 1′. That is the useful boundary here; UEFA's accounts differ over the exact second.

An early goal does not describe everything that follows. Liverpool's first-half record will include attempts of their own, and the eventual interval figures should not be read as evidence that they never threatened. For now, the change is precise and substantial: all eleven starters remain on each side, but Milan hold the lead.

Vladimír Šmicer replaces Kewell in the 23rd minute. Liverpool's attack changes before the score changes again. Kewell later recalled leaving through injury; the contemporary UEFA account also describes him pulling up. The personnel record establishes the replacement, while those accounts supply the reason.

This is Liverpool's first substitution. Under the rules in use for this match they may make three, without re-entry: Kewell cannot come back on. Šmicer is therefore part of the side that reaches the interval. Any explanation of the half-time decision must begin with that changed XI, rather than with the team sheet issued before kick-off.

Crespo makes it 0–2 in the 39th minute. Milan move forward, Kaká finds Shevchenko and the striker squares for Crespo to finish. The sequence connects Milan's creative player with both forwards; the goal record identifies Crespo as the scorer. Liverpool's task has grown from finding an equaliser to recovering a two-goal deficit.

The later tactical analysis focuses on the space Milan could use through the middle. That is an interpretation of how the attack developed, rather than a measured map of the players' positions. The firmer ground is the passing sequence described in the contemporary account and the second goal now recorded against Liverpool.

Five minutes after his first, Crespo scores again. Kaká supplies the pass through to him, and the official record places the goal at 44′. Milan take a three-goal lead towards half-time. The second and third goals have arrived close together, but they remain separate moments: first a two-goal problem, then a three-goal one.

The interval has not yet brought a chance to reorganise. Liverpool still have Šmicer in Kewell's place and Finnan on the field. Those details matter because the next change will involve a player who started in defence and a substitute who can alter the midfield. The score tells Benítez what must be recovered; the available personnel constrain how he can attempt it.

moments.title: Half-time: the problem and the options

blocks.text: At half-time Liverpool trail 0–3. Šmicer has already replaced Kewell, leaving two substitutions available. Finnan remains in the interval XI. Hamann, Cissé, Carson, Josemi, Núñez and Bišćan are the six unused named substitutes. That is the bench from which the next change can be made; it is not proof that every player is fully fit. Kewell is no longer an option under the no-re-entry rule.

Finnan's injury adds a constraint that the team list alone cannot show. In Liverpool FC's later player recollections, Finnan describes being injured and receiving treatment; Hamann recalls learning that Finnan, rather than Traoré, would be the player replaced. These are attributed memories recorded a decade later. They help explain the choice, but should not be presented as a verbatim record of everything said in the dressing room.

The first-half figures give another view of the situation. UEFA records Liverpool with five shots, one 'shot on goal' and 44 per cent possession, against Milan's seven, five and 56 per cent. The report describes the completed half. It does not establish that Benítez had this exact statistical sheet available during the break, and the counts cannot measure the quality of every opportunity. They do prevent a loose claim that Liverpool had offered no threat at all.

The tactical question is how to add an attacking threat without leaving the centre exposed. Liverpool FC's 2015 analysis interprets the change as three defenders behind a midfield strengthened by Hamann, with Gerrard able to move further forward. The comparison below separates the interval personnel from the restart. Selecting the second view does not move the match on: it shows the proposed answer alongside the problem. Both views are schematics, not tracking data or evidence that players occupied fixed coordinates. The change is Hamann for Finnan before the restart, leaving Liverpool one substitution.

blocks.title: Compare the interval with the restart

blocks.text: Hamann replaces Finnan before the second half begins. Liverpool restart at 0–3 with one substitution left. The actual exchange of players is established by UEFA's report, which records the change at 46′; 'second-half restart' describes the boundary without inventing an elapsed second.

The labels used to explain the new shape differ. Liverpool FC's retrospective analysis calls it 3-4-2-1; the surrounding analysis in Sky Sports' later account uses 3-5-2. Neither label changes who has come on or gone off. The important explanatory connection is Hamann's presence in midfield and the opportunity for Gerrard to operate further forward. The diagram follows the club analysis while keeping that attribution visible.

Gerrard heads in Riise's cross in the 54th minute. Liverpool have their first goal: 1–3. It reduces the deficit to two and gives a concrete expression to the captain's attacking involvement after the restart. Milan still lead, and Liverpool still need two more goals simply to draw level.

Šmicer scores from outside the penalty area two minutes later. The substitute who entered before half-time now makes it 2–3. Liverpool have cut the gap to one. His shot is a separate step in the recovery, after Gerrard's header and before the penalty incident that will offer another opportunity.

Liverpool are awarded a penalty for Gattuso's foul on Gerrard. Dida saves Alonso's kick, but Alonso follows in and scores from the rebound at 60′. The match is level at 3–3. The goal is the rebound, not a successful penalty: this sequence belongs to open match play, wholly separate from the later shoot-out.

moments.title: Level, with the match still to resolve

blocks.text: Drawing level does not decide the final. Liverpool and Milan still have the remainder of normal time to play. The score stays at 3–3 while further personnel changes reshape the contest. Carragher is booked at 76′ and Baroš at 81′; these are recorded disciplinary events, not additional goals or substitutions.

At 85′ Cissé replaces Baroš and Tomasson replaces Crespo. Both changes have the same official minute; their order in the record here does not claim to resolve which happened first within it. Liverpool have now used all three substitutions. Milan bring on Serginho for Seedorf at 86′, the minute given by UEFA. The named unused players remain visible, but Liverpool cannot turn those names into further changes under this match's rules.

Normal time ends with the teams still level at 3–3. Liverpool have recovered the three goals conceded in the first half, but neither side has won the match. The final proceeds to extra time, with two further periods to be played before penalties become necessary if the score remains equal.

There is no additional substitute awarded for extra time under the rules used here. Liverpool enter it having made all three changes. The match score at this boundary is known; the statistics available in UEFA's report are first-half figures and totals including extra time. Those later totals cannot be relabelled as the position after ninety minutes.

The score remains 3–3 into extra time. Milan make their final substitution at 112′, Rui Costa replacing Gattuso. Liverpool's available on-field personnel have not changed since Cissé came on. Both sides have now used their three substitutions.

Later accounts describe Gerrard taking a deeper role on Liverpool's right in response to Serginho. The role detail shows that relationship, using players eligible at this late boundary. It is deliberately partial: it does not invent a complete extra-time formation or claim that the adjustment began at the instant Rui Costa entered. Gerrard's earlier attacking contribution and this later defensive responsibility belong to different stages of the same final.

Late in extra time, Dudek makes a double save from Shevchenko. He stops the first effort and the immediate follow-up, keeping the match level. UEFA's contemporary report places the intervention near the end of extra time; the account here retains that approximate timing instead of assigning an unsupported exact timestamp.

The consequence is a preserved 3–3, not a victory already secured. A Milan goal would have changed the score, but extra time was not being played under a rule that stopped the match as soon as a goal was scored. Dudek's intervention keeps Liverpool level as the final approaches its next method of resolution.

After 120 minutes the match is still 3–3. The shoot-out begins with Milan taking first. Match goals and shoot-out goals are counted separately: the original score will stay 3–3 while the penalty tally changes with each attempt.

Follow the kicks one at a time to see what each result leaves possible. Each side initially has five attempts, but the contest ends as soon as the trailing side can no longer draw level with its remaining kicks. An unsuccessful attempt changes that calculation even though it adds no goal. The full record is also available for reference; opening it does not advance the sequence.

Dudek saves Shevchenko's attempt and the shoot-out ends with Liverpool ahead 3–2. Milan have taken five kicks and Liverpool four. No fifth Liverpool attempt is required: Milan have no kick left with which to recover the deficit. The match result remains 3–3 after extra time, with Liverpool winning on penalties.

Liverpool are European champions for the fifth time. The recovery from 0–3 made the later contest possible; it did not remove the need to finish normal time, withstand extra time and complete the shoot-out. The final statistics below cover the whole 120 minutes, excluding penalties. From here, the existing season and Benítez era pages place the evening back within the club's wider history.
Fourteen matches, including qualifying, brought Liverpool to the final. Scores below are Liverpool first; home and away refer to Liverpool.
Liverpool progressed 2–1 on aggregate.
Liverpool finished as group runners-up.

Liverpool beat Chelsea 1–0 on aggregate.
